# What it is, goals and examples



A dose-response meta-analysis pools studies to estimate how an outcome changes
across levels of an exposure, rather than between two groups. The output is not
a single number. It is a curve, with a confidence band, over the exposure range
the evidence actually covers.

That shift from number to curve is the whole subject. Everything in this chapter
follows from it.

## What a dose-response meta-analysis is

A standard meta-analysis takes one effect estimate per study and pools them.
Each study contributes a comparison: treated against control, exposed against
unexposed. The result answers one question, "does it matter", and answers it at
whatever dose the studies happened to use.

A dose-response meta-analysis takes *several* estimates per study, one for each
exposure level, and pools the relationship running through them. Study A might
report risk at 0, 10 and 20 units. Study B might report 0, 15 and 30. Neither
alone has enough points to describe a curve with confidence. Together, and with
the right handling of the fact that estimates within a study share a reference
group, they do.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![What a standard meta-analysis produces from four studies: one estimate each, pooled into a single summary. Drawn with `meta::forest()` so it is the plot this literature already knows how to read. The numbers are schematic.](01-what-is-it_files/figure-html/fig-standard-ma-1.png){#fig-standard-ma fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


Every study contributes one row, and the diamond at the foot is the answer. Now
compare what the same four studies look like when each of them reports several
exposure levels rather than one contrast.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![What a dose-response meta-analysis produces from the same kind of evidence. Each dotted line is one study, with a point per exposure level it reported; the solid line is the relationship pooled across them. There is no single row per study here, and no diamond, because the answer is a curve. Schematic.](01-what-is-it_files/figure-html/fig-dose-response-data-1.png){#fig-dose-response-data fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


The method originates with @greenland1992, who showed that the covariance
between estimates within a study can be reconstructed from the published table,
and that a trend can then be fitted by generalised least squares. Every method
in this book is a descendant of that result.

::: {.callout-note}
The exposure must be quantitative and comparable across studies. "Dose" need not
mean a drug. It can be minutes of exercise per week, grams of processed meat per
day, or years of follow-up. What it cannot be is a category with no natural
ordering.
:::

## What it answers

Three questions, none of which a pooled estimate can answer.

**Does the effect grow with the dose?** A single estimate tells you the average
effect across whatever doses were studied. It cannot tell you whether that
average hides a strong effect at high doses and nothing at low ones.

**Is there a threshold, or a ceiling?** Many interventions stop paying off past
some point. A pooled estimate reports the average of the paying and the
not-paying region, which describes neither.

**What dose would you actually recommend?** This is the question clinicians and
guideline committees ask, and it is unanswerable without a curve.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![The three questions a curve answers and a single estimate cannot. The threshold is where the effect separates from the null, the ceiling is where further dose stops buying benefit, and the recommended dose is an argument about where on the curve to stand. The dashed horizontal line is what a standard meta-analysis would have reported for the same evidence. Schematic.](01-what-is-it_files/figure-html/fig-what-it-answers-1.png){#fig-what-it-answers fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


## The shapes a curve can take

Readers do not argue about coefficients. They argue about shape, so it is worth
having the names straight before fitting anything.

A **positive association** rises across the whole observed range: more exposure,
more effect, with no sign of levelling. An **inverse association** is its mirror.

An **Emax** curve rises and then flattens. The name comes from pharmacology,
where the maximum achievable effect is reached and further dose adds nothing.
This is the shape behind most "no additional benefit beyond X" recommendations.

A **non-monotonic** curve turns: it rises, peaks, and comes back down. The
antidepressant dose-response literature is the standard example
[@furukawa2019], where higher doses eventually cost more in dropout than they
return in benefit.

**No association** is a flat curve whose band contains the null throughout. It
is a real finding and worth reporting, because "we looked for a dose-response
relationship and found none" is more informative than a pooled estimate that was
never going to show one.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![The five shapes, one panel each. The dashed line is the null. The names follow the literature: a curve that rises throughout is a positive association, one that rises and then flattens is an Emax curve, and one that turns is non-monotonic. These are exactly the labels `curve_shape()` returns. Schematic.](01-what-is-it_files/figure-html/fig-curve-shapes-1.png){#fig-curve-shapes fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


The `easyDR` package will name a fitted curve for you, so a results paragraph
can use the same vocabulary as the literature:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(easyDR)

curve_shape(dose = 0:4, effect = c(0, 0.20, 0.40, 0.60, 0.80))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "positive association"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
curve_shape(dose = 0:4, effect = c(0, 0.50, 0.80, 0.85, 0.86))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Emax"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
curve_shape(dose = 0:4, effect = c(0, 0.50, 0.90, 0.40, -0.10))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "non-monotonic"
```


:::
:::


## Why it is not a network meta-analysis

A network meta-analysis can include several doses of the same drug by treating
each dose as a separate node. It will then rank those nodes. This looks like a
dose-response answer and is not one.

The ranking tells you which of the studied doses performed best. It does not
estimate the relationship *between* them, so it cannot interpolate to a dose
nobody trialled, and it cannot describe a shape. Treating 10 mg and 20 mg as
unrelated categories discards the one fact that makes them comparable: that 20
is twice 10.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![What a network meta-analysis actually produces, drawn with `netmeta::netsplit()` on the Senn2013 diabetes network. For every pair of treatments it reports the direct evidence, the indirect evidence routed through the rest of the network, and the network estimate combining the two, then asks whether direct and indirect agree. Every row is a pair of nodes. Nothing in the model knows that one node might be twice the dose of another, so no row describes a shape.](01-what-is-it_files/figure-html/fig-nma-netsplit-1.png){#fig-nma-netsplit fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


Node splitting is the check that makes a network trustworthy, and it is worth
knowing for its own sake. It is also the clearest demonstration of the gap: the
whole apparatus is about whether two routes to the same comparison agree, and
never about what happens between the doses.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![The same four doses, read as a dose-response question. The ordering is now information rather than labels, which is what lets the model say anything about the gaps between the studied doses. Schematic.](01-what-is-it_files/figure-html/fig-nma-vs-dr-1.png){#fig-nma-vs-dr fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


Model-based network meta-analysis closes this gap deliberately, by fitting a
dose-response function inside the network [@mawdsley2016; @pedder2021]. That is
a dose-response method wearing network clothing, and it is the right tool when
the evidence is a network. Ordinary network meta-analysis is not.

## Why it is not a meta-regression or a subgroup analysis

**Meta-regression** puts dose on the right-hand side of a regression across
studies. It is the closest relative, and the difference matters: meta-regression
usually relates one effect estimate per study to the average dose in that study,
which makes it vulnerable to aggregation bias and restricts it in practice to a
straight line. A dose-response meta-analysis uses the within-study comparisons
across levels, which is where the information about shape lives.

**Subgroup analysis** splits studies into low, medium and high and pools each.
You get three numbers and no relationship between them. Nothing constrains them
to lie on any curve, nothing uses the ordering, and the cut points are usually
arbitrary.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Three ways to put dose on the x-axis. Meta-regression uses one point per study at its average dose and fits a line through them. Subgroup analysis pools within arbitrary bands and leaves three unconnected numbers. Only the dose-response model uses the within-study comparisons, drawn here as the dotted segments, which is where the information about shape lives. Schematic.](01-what-is-it_files/figure-html/fig-not-metareg-1.png){#fig-not-metareg fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


What all three alternatives share is that they ignore the common comparator.
Within a study, every exposure level is compared against the same reference
group, which makes the estimates correlated. That correlation is a nuisance to
be handled, and handling it correctly is exactly what @greenland1992 made
possible.

## What the published examples look like

Three papers worth reading before writing your own protocol.

**Physical activity and mortality** [@garcia2023]. A two-stage analysis in
`dosresmeta` with restricted cubic splines, pooling large prospective cohorts of
non-occupational physical activity against cardiovascular disease, cancer and
mortality. The analysis code is published, so it can be re-run rather than
merely read. This is the worked example used in Chapter 4.

**Optimal antidepressant dose** [@furukawa2019]. A dose-response meta-analysis
of double-blind randomised trials of SSRIs, venlafaxine and mirtazapine, asking
not whether the drugs work but what dose to aim for. The clearest published case
of benefit and tolerability pulling in opposite directions as dose climbs, which
is what makes the curve turn.

**The Burden of Proof studies** [@gbd2022tobacco; @gbd2022vegetables]. A
different toolchain, a different modelling philosophy, and an instructive public
dispute about whether the modelling choices drive the conclusions
[@burdenofproofconcerns2023]. Read the critique alongside the papers. Chapter 5
returns to it, because it is the best available lesson in how a dose-response
result can be over-read.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![The shape each worked example reports, drawn to comparable axes. Benefit accrues fast and then levels off for physical activity, turns against higher doses for antidepressants, and keeps climbing with a band wide enough to argue about in the Burden of Proof studies. These are schematic redrawings of the reported shapes, not the published estimates; go to the papers for those.](01-what-is-it_files/figure-html/fig-published-shapes-1.png){#fig-published-shapes fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


## Should you use it?

Run a dose-response meta-analysis when all of these hold:

1. The exposure is quantitative, and the levels can be put on a common scale
   across studies.
2. Enough studies report at least three exposure levels. Two-stage methods need
   three; one-stage methods can use studies with fewer [@crippa2019], so failing
   this test argues for one-stage rather than for giving up.
3. Each study compares its levels against a common reference group, and reports
   enough per level to reconstruct the covariance: counts, group sizes, and the
   estimate with its interval.
4. The shape is the question. If you only want to know whether the exposure
   matters at all, a standard meta-analysis answers that with less machinery.

Do not run one when doses cannot be harmonised, when almost every study reports
a single contrast, or when the exposure is categorical in nature.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Condition 2, read off an extraction sheet. Each bar is one study's count of exposure levels; the dashed line is the three-level floor a two-stage fit needs. Studies below it are dropped by two-stage methods and kept by one-stage, so a sheet that looks like this argues for one-stage rather than for abandoning the review. Schematic.](01-what-is-it_files/figure-html/fig-viability-1.png){#fig-viability fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


Chapter 2 turns this list into a check you can run against a real extraction
sheet, and `easyDR::dr_viability()` performs it:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
d <- data.frame(
  study = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B"),
  dose  = c(0, 10, 20, 0, 15),
  cases = c(10, 20, 31, 5, 9),
  n     = c(100, 100, 100, 50, 50)
)

dr_viability(d)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Dose-response viability

  study levels has_reference two_stage_ok
1     A      3          TRUE         TRUE
2     B      2          TRUE        FALSE

Problems:
 - 1 study(ies) with fewer than 3 exposure levels (B): a two-stage fit drops these. Consider one-stage.
```


:::
:::


Study B has two levels, so a two-stage fit would silently drop it. Knowing that
before extraction finishes is worth more than knowing it afterwards.

## What you will be able to do

By the end of this book you will be able to state a dose-response question
precisely, judge from an extraction sheet whether the evidence can support one,
fit and interpret the model, and read a published dose-response curve critically
enough to see where its author went past what the data supports.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}

:::
